recorded: 11 April 1950, Columbia 30th Street Studio, New York; LP published 1951
question: When does a finger exercise begin to sound like a daydream?
intro: An apparently dutiful keyboard exercise acquires a wandering middle and an exuberant finish. Debussy asks for evenness “without dryness”: follow the difference between the running notes and the larger phrases they carry.

sections.label: A · The exercise
sections.mNote: running semiquavers surround slower melodic notes

sections.label: B · A wandering respite
sections.mNote: longer notes and changing harmony interrupt the exercise

sections.label: A′ · Exercise and acceleration
sections.mNote: opening figuration returns and grows into an animated finish

cues.title: Even, but not dry
cues.text: The opening instruction asks for an even touch “without dryness”. Listen beyond the running semiquavers: slower notes give them a melodic direction, so the passage is more than a stream of equally important attacks.
cues.evidence: Viewed Durand score, plate D. & F. 7188, printed pp. 1–2: égal et sans sécheresse, running figures and sustained notes. The analysis report places the opening rise in level at 0:05–0:15; no particular finger, pedal movement or individual attack is identified. Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/0d/IMSLP252526-PMLP02387-Debussy%2C_Claude-Childrens_Corner_Durand_7188_filter.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A father’s tender apology
cues.text: Debussy dedicated the six pieces to his daughter Chouchou, with “her father’s tender apologies for what follows”. The dedication makes this a suite offered to a child, not a claim that its intricate piano writing is a beginner’s exercise.
cues.evidence: The viewed dedication leaf reads À ma chère petite Chouchou, avec les tendres excuses de son Père pour ce qui va suivre. The English wording is our translation; no claim about a particular childhood incident is made. Durand score, PDF p. 2: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/0d/IMSLP252526-PMLP02387-Debussy%2C_Claude-Childrens_Corner_Durand_7188_filter.pdf

cues.title: Recovering the running figure
cues.text: Through the brief respite and the return, compare the longer, more hesitant phrases with the original stream of notes. The exercise becomes recognisable again through its pattern of movement, not just through a louder sound.
cues.evidence: The report has strong changes at 0:50, 0:54, 1:00 and 1:14, with quieter windows at 0:55 and 1:10. Viewed score pp. 3–4 supplies the contrasting passage and 1° Tempo return. The 1:14 boundary is an approximate passage anchor, not an aligned bar.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The exercise breaks loose
cues.text: Near the end, Debussy asks the pianist to become progressively more animated, then very animated. The running figure drives towards firm closing chords: the exercise finishes with an energy quite unlike its restrained beginning.
cues.evidence: Viewed score pp. 4–5: En animant peu à peu, Très animé and the final C-major chords. The report’s loudest five-second windows lie between 1:25 and 1:45, before a marked fall after 1:50. These anchors support the broad closing build, not a measured tempo curve.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The exercise loses its straight course
transitions.how: The C-major exercise gives way to a less regular exchange of running figures, held notes and rests. Debussy changes the written key signatures and lets the phrases linger, so the bass no longer supports one continuous sweep of semiquavers. The connection is still pianistic movement: fragments of the exercise survive inside the more expressive passage. Listen for interrupted momentum rather than a new tune arriving with a decisive cadence.
transitions.evidence: Viewed Durand score, printed p. 3, supplies the longer notes, rests, altered key signatures and flexible pace. The report finds changes at 0:50 and 0:54 and a low-level window at 0:55. The join is estimated from those anchors; no timestamped modulation or bar number is claimed.

transitions.title: The first pattern gathers fresh speed
transitions.how: After the held-back phrase, 1° Tempo restores the opening’s running pattern and C-major framework. The return does not merely repeat the start: Debussy soon asks for increasing animation, takes the figure through a wider register and builds towards the forceful ending. A familiar texture supplies the recognition; its growing pace and weight supply the changed character.
transitions.evidence: The strongest reported change is at 1:14; the quiet 1:10 window is followed by increasing level through 1:25–1:45. Viewed score pp. 4–5 supplies 1° Tempo, the restored figuration and progressive animation. The timing is passage-level, not bar-aligned.

composer.epithet: He made a chord’s spacing, a scale’s missing notes and an instrument’s register determine the course of a piece.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
French Symbolist poetry · Russian music · Javanese gamelan · eighteenth-century French keyboard music
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, outside Paris. Neither parent was a professional musician. His father’s involvement in the Paris Commune brought imprisonment in 1871; through a connection made during that imprisonment, the boy came to the piano teacher Antoinette Mauté, Verlaine’s mother-in-law. He entered the Paris Conservatoire in 1872, aged ten. Antoine Marmontel trained him as a pianist; Ernest Guiraud later taught him composition. His resistance to harmonic rules developed inside this education: he could play, analyse and compete successfully in the system he came to distrust.

From 1880 he spent summers working for Nadezhda von Meck, Tchaikovsky’s patron, playing chamber music and teaching her children. Travel with her household took him to Italy and Russia. In Paris he accompanied the soprano Marie Vasnier, with whom he had an affair, and wrote songs for her flexible high voice. In their accompaniments, the piano’s register, resonance and passing harmonic changes can supply a second interpretation of the words. The early songs also show how thoroughly he knew the French vocal tradition he would alter.
